newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil deputies to resume voting on reform bill.
newsitem.headline: Brazil deputies to resume voting on reform bill.

text.p: Brazil's Chamber of Deputies was set to resume voting on the government's civil service reform bill later Wednesday with several of the legislation's key points under threat.

Government allies and opposition members have proposed more than 100 amendments to the controversial reform. Last week, the bill survived a first vote in the lower house with just one vote more than the three-fifths majority of 308 it needed.

Earlier this week, however, the government withdrew support for an amendment entitling lawmakers to a pay ceiling twice as high as other public sector workers, throwing in doubt its ability to muster enough support for the reform now.
The government needs three-fifths majorities to kill several amendments which would remove key elements of the reform.
Key points of the reform which could be reversed include:
-- the possibility of dismissing workers whose jobs are currently protected by the constitution;

-- the creation of a new category of public sector workers who would enjoy only restricted benefits. Currently, all workers are entitled to the same rights, including automatic pay rises to match increases awarded elsewhere in the civil service;
-- a "sub-ceiling" allowing states and municipalities to cap pay and pensions at a rate lower than that set for federal workers.
Leaders of government-allied parties were due to meet around midday Wednesday to discuss the possibility of postponing the voting on the amendments, a congressional official said.

An estimated 140 deputies in the 513-member lower house earn pensions from previous civil service posts and would lose out in the 10,800 real ($10,188) monthly ceiling on pay and pensions as proposed in the reform.
Their opposition would jeopardise the government's attempts to defeat the amendments and approve the reform when it is put to its second vote in the lower house.

However, newspapers said the government's cause might be helped by a loophole in the text of the reform which fixes the ceiling according to the salary of judges on the Supreme Federal Tribunal (STF), Brazil's highest paid public sector workers.

Although the monthly salary of the STF judges is 10,800 reais, the court's president Sepulveda Pertence revealed Tuesday that some members earn an extra 1,920 reais a month for work they do in a federal electoral court.
The newspapers said that fact could lead to the ceiling being increased to 12,720 reais a month, perhaps soothing irate members of Congress.
The government also has another trump card -- an amendment which would grant automatic pay rises to the ceiling's limit for lawmakers, whose salary is currently 8,000 reais a month.
The increase would be introduced via decree once the reform has been fully approved in Congress.
